small.text: Look down the next time you step out your door.  There's a road under you.  You use roads so often that you never ask where they come from.  You save that for old things, and roads don't feel old to you.  They feel like they belong to cars, trucks, freight.  So who built the first roads and why?  You'll probably reach for one of three, the Romans, or traders moving goods, or  no one, until someone had a wheel.  All three feel right.  All three, as far as we can tell, are wrong.  The earliest road builders we can name weren't fighting distance.  They were fighting water.  water. Their land was going soft under their feet, so they built it a floor.  To see what that means, you need to stand in a bog. A bog is land that never dries.  Rain sits on dead moss, new moss grows over it, and the ground turns into a wet sponge.  It will take your boot and it can take you. You can't farm it, you can't cross it.  Almost 6,000 years ago, in what's now Somerset in the south of England, people  face the same ground you'd sink in. And they built.  We call what they built the sweet track. Tree rings pin its date. Each year a tree  adds one ring, wide in a good year, thin in a bad one, and you can match that pattern  against a known series.  The result, 3807 BC or 3806, because the trees were felled in winter, one winter spans two  calendar years, and even the wood can't tell you which.  And what stood there was no trail.  It was a structure, about 1800 meters of walkway across a reed marsh, from an island  at West Hay to a ridge at Shapwick.  Oak planks up to 40 centimeters wide, 3 meters long, less than 5 centimeters thick,  split, not sawn, out of oaks up to 400 years old and a meter through.  The tool kit, stone axes, wooden wedges, wooden mallets, that's all.  They drove crossed pegs of ash, oak, and lime into the peat, the bogs packed dead plants,  laid long rails of hazel and alder, cut notches into the planks, and slotted the parts together.  No nails.  A push fit.  And the pegs are so straight and clean that the wood points to a managed stand.  Trees cut low and regrown on cycles for at least 120 years before this was built.  Now hold on to the strangest part.  All that effort bought a walkway of single oak planks, late end to end, not a cart track,  a plank line through a marsh.  It served for about ten years, then the water rose again and took it.  And under it runs an older line still, the post track, from around 3838 BC, same route  thirty years earlier.  They had done this before.  One site might be a fluke, so go northeast to the flat wet country of Lower Saxony  in northern Germany.  More than 550 wooden paths are known there.  laid across bogs and soaked ground, from the Stone Age into modern times,  and beside one of those paths, Diggers found a thing that had no business being there.  Hold on to that. We'll come back for it.  Some of the oldest paths sit near a lake called the Deemer.  One of them, a path labeled PR-31, crossed a bog called the Kham Poo Moor.  It's around six and a half thousand years old.  The studies differ on the exact years, so hold that number loosely.  It ran up to four and a half meters wide, and it had layers,  thin birch trunks at the bottom, three rows of pine logs as a base,  base, a surface of pine logs up to 20 cm thick pinned along the edges with birch pegs.  Base, bed, surface.  That is road engineering, done with stone axes.  The chop marks are still on the ends of the logs, and 30 meters to one side, there runs  a second path, laid roughly 1700 years later.  Same bog, same problem, same answer.  Why there?  Why then?  The team behind the newest study says it with care.  It's one paper and they call their reading a hypothesis, but it goes like this.  The rain grew, the lake rose, the wet spread, and the paths follow that curve.  PR 31, they write, was created in a phase of increasing water logging.  They point to a second driver, too.  People were settling in new patterns.  So even here, water isn't the whole story.  But zoom out, and the paths seem to come in waves, building booms that track the  ground getting worse.  One more trace, and it's an odd one.  pollen from the bog shows the pine stands shrinking after that second path was built.  The likely cause is the wood the builders took.  a forest shrinking because the road was being built.  Now the thing that had no business being there.  By one of these paths, PR7, laid in the 25th century BC, Diggers found it.  Two broken wagon axles.  They count among the oldest evidence of wheels and wagons in all of northern Germany.  So run the numbers with me.  Oldest known road in that region?  About six and a half thousand years old.  Oldest known wheels?  About four and a half thousand.  The road wins by roughly two thousand years.  People there built roads for some 20 centuries before anything rolled on one.  One axle lay broken next to the path, right there in the bog.  The wheel is not the parent of the road. The wheel is a guest on it.  So if the first roads weren't for wheels and weren't for goods, what were roads for?  Chase that question around the world and you get a new answer at every stop.  And the answers are stranger than you'd think.  Start in Egypt about 4,500 years ago.  In the desert southwest of what's now Cairo, a paved road runs some 11 kilometers.  The reports differ a little on the length, from a quarry, a pit where you cut stone,  down to what was then the shore of a lake.  The quarry is called Wiedan El Farras, and the paving is whatever lay close, basalt,  a hard dark lava stone, limestone, sandstone, and slabs of petrified wood, dead trees  turned to stone, latest pavement.  The road's job?  No market anywhere.  where. Crews hauled basalt blocks down it to the water and shipped them off to become  temple floors for the pyramids. One of those floors sits just east of the Great Pyramid  at Giza. Even here, the road was only the hard leg of the trip. The blocks moved mostly  by boat, in seasons when the lake stood high. This road was a supply drive for a  royal building site. Walls of glazed brick, and on them lions, bulls, and dragons,  about 120 figures glowing on yellow and black, lining a street in Babylon. This  This is in what's now Iraq, around 569 BC, under King Nebuchadnezzar II.  The street itself is stone slab, set in a bed of bitumen, natural tar, up to 20 meters  wide at some points.  Picture yourself walking it.  From the river through the temple district, past the palaces, to the Ishtar Gate, the  city's great blue gate.  People used it all year.  It was the main axis of the city.  But the day it was dressed for came once a year.  At the spring new year, statues of the gods were carried through the gate and  down the street in a grand procession.  All of it, the tar, the lions, the glaze, was at heart a stage.  Persia, roughly modern Iran, gets one breath, a road of about 2,700 kilometers.  Suso to Sardis, ridden in nine days with fresh horses waiting along the way, walked in 90.  A post road, the record says, it moved messages, it ran an empire.  And then there's the road nobody can explain.  Chaco Canyon, New Mexico, in the dry southwest of the United States, roughly a thousand  years back, though the dating is argued over.  The people there had no wheel, no horse, no ox, yet they scraped roadbeds into the desert  floor up to 9 meters wide, dead straight.  One of them runs 50.5 kilometers.  Where a cliff stood in the way, they cut stone stairs into the rock face and went  straight over.  Nothing ever rolled here.  So why the width?  Why the line?  The honest answer?  Nobody knows.  Scholars have argued for decades, work, war, worship, politics.  A recent laser survey found roads lined up on the midwinter sunrise over a mountain  sacred to the native Pueblo peoples today, a hint toward ritual and still one reading among several.  We can map these roads from the air. We can't tell you what they were for.  Last stop, the Andes, the long mountain spine of South America. The Inca empire ran a road net  whose true size nobody can state. Estimates go from 23,000 to 60,000 kilometers. Parts are  older than the empire, laid by earlier peoples, the Wari and the Tiwanaku. It was paved only  where paving earned its keep. Elsewhere it was packed earth and sand. Its builders had  no wheel and no animal to pull a cart, so where the land climbed, the road did what  no cart road can do. It became a staircase. Stairs stop a wheel cold. For you on foot,  they are simply the shortest way up. On this net, an empire moved on foot, and today,  only about a quarter of it is still visible at all.  Which brings us, at the very end, to trade, and to Rome. You were promised the Romans.  Romans. Here they are, in last place. Rome's first great road, the Appian Way, was begun  in 312 BC as a military road, in the middle of a war, to move troops south, not a trade  route. And the picture book Roman Road, that deep stack of stone layers? Even in Rome  it was the top class, not the rule. Roman law sorted roads into three kinds, and two  of them were plain earth and gravel. Trade is the answer you'd expect, and the one  that keeps not showing up. That doesn't mean traders never walk these paths. It means trade  moved in later, like the wheel did, into a thing that was already old.  So here's the thought to keep. A road was never only about speed. A road is a promise.  The ground will hold, and the way will still be there tomorrow, in the wet season, in  the dark. People in a Somerset Marsh made that promise with stone axes almost 6,000  years back, and kept it through 10 years of rising water. And in that German bog  country, the oldest road and the oldest wheel we've found lie about 2,000 years apart road first.  So the next time the ground under you goes soft you know what humans do.  They did it before the wheel. They did it before Rome. They look at land that says no and they build a yes.
